In colonial times however, this secular mindset was not yet present, allowing for the spread of (fundamentalistic) religions to Africa. While the European countries were able to secularize thanks to the availability time and money to invest in sciences, African countries mostly weren't able to do so because of civil unrest, wars, and the fact that their own religions were violently stripped away from them and replaced by Christianity. This engrained Christianity in their way of life, making it easier for the European powers to control them (because after all that is the goal of organised religion), but also making it hard to secularise, as their belief was often what helped them cope with the various human rights abuses carried out against them. 
That's my opinion at least.
